https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-launches-o.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ityt Ukraine has increasingly stepped up its attacks on infrastructure within Russia (FILE: 16:08:2026) Image: Stringer/REUTERS Advertisement Hundreds of drones targeted the Moscow region in a sustained overnight assault that killed at least six people, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as Ukraine steps up long-range attacks deep inside Russia. Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 600 drones had been flying toward the Moscow region between Saturday evening and 6:30 a.m. local time (0330 UTC) on Sunday, adding that 201 were destroyed over the region. What happened in Moscow drone attack? Russia said five people had been killed in Ukraine's attacks, five in the southwestern city of Rostov and one in the Moscow region. Sobyanin said three people were wounded in the area inside Moscow's MKAD ring road and were receiving medical treatment. Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes inside Russia in recent weeks, targeting military and industrial facilities as well as warehouses far from the front line. Ukraine's Kyiv Independent newspaper reported that Ukrainian forces had targeted a warehouse belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries as well as industrial facilities in several cities across the Moscow region. There was no immediate independent confirmation of the scale of the attack. Where did Russia attack in Ukraine? Russian attacks have killed at least five people and wounded dozens more across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian officials. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a missile strike on his hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people and injured 14 others, while another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy. How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy said the Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih caused multiple casualties, with emergency services responding at the scene. The city, a major industrial center in central Ukraine, has repeatedly been targeted during the war. In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed when a Russian strike hit their home, regional military administration head Ivan Fedorov said. Spanish fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania The attack came as NATO countries on Ukraine's borders faced fresh drone incursions of their own. Romania's Defense Ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone early Sunday after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near the border with Ukraine. The aircraft was operating on NATO duties and intercepted the drone at 5:01 a.m. local time (0201 UTC). Debris fell in an unpopulated area of Galati county, close to the Ukrainian border. Romanian authorities did not immediately identify the drone's origin or say who launched it. Romania has repeatedly reported drone debris on its territory since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube. On Friday, an Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command also shot down a foreign drone that entered Latvian airspace . Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/.text: Military Menu Introduction Systems Facilities Agencies Industry Operations Countries Hot Documents News Reports Policy Budget Congress Links WMD Intelligence Homeland Security Space Military Minister Pevkur in Stockholm: Closer cooperation with Sweden strengthens security across the region Republic of Estonia - Ministry of Defence 21.08.2026 Estonian Minister of Defence Hanno Pevkur met with Swedish Minister for Defence Pål Jonson in Stockholm to discuss strengthening defence cooperation between Estonia and Sweden, the defence of NATO's eastern flank, and enhancing regional security. "Sweden's accession to NATO has significantly strengthened security across the region and provided an even stronger foundation for our defence cooperation. Sweden clearly understands the danger posed by Russia and takes the defence of Europe and NATO's eastern flank very seriously. We also hope that airspace restrictions will soon be lifted, allowing Swedish aircraft to operate, if necessary, without restrictions in the airspace of other NATO member states. Estonia, for its part, has taken all necessary steps to ensure that there are no restrictions on Swedish aircraft entering our airspace," said Minister of Defence Hanno Pevkur. "We are also equally committed to continued support for Ukraine. This year, both Estonia and Sweden are directing more than 0.25 per cent of GDP towards military support for Ukraine, and we call on all Allies to do the same. Sweden is supporting Ukraine with as much as 0.5 per cent of its GDP. Sweden has also set a firm goal of increasing its defence spending," Pevkur said. Sweden has made a significant contribution to the IT Coalition, led by Estonia and Luxembourg, as well as to the procurement of weapons for Ukraine through the PURL mechanism. Sweden has also joined the Legio support mechanism led by Poland, under which Ukraine is supported through the delivery of weapons and equipment as well as the training of Ukrainian defence personnel. Sweden also participates in the European Union's Eastern Flank Watch initiative, under which it works closely with Lithuania, Latvia, Poland and Finland. Pevkur also met with the Estonian community in Stockholm. "I am pleased to see how deeply the security of Estonia matters to Estonians living abroad and how willing they are to find ways to contribute to their homeland," the Minister commented. In addition, the Minister met with Peter Hultqvist, Chair of the Swedish Parliament's Defence Committee, and took part in the "Unleashed" conference on the future and cooperation of the Nordic and Baltic countries.

Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA View image in fullscreen Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA Yemen Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports Violence in Yemen: why it matters and how it is linked to the US-Iran war Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes. The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday. Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday. The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait. View image in fullscreen Fighters loyal to the Houthi rebels march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated. Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014. British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967. The surge in fighting in the past week had sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday. View image in fullscreen Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday. The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy. Map of Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers. On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble. Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces. View image in fullscreen A view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast. Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason. Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back. Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran. There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence. Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Chan, who was jailed for 18 years in February, was described by prosecutors as a ‘prolific sexual predator’. Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty Images Children Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry Sirin Kale Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested. In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences , including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”. The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan. Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery. Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care. After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, north London , including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison. The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate. In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025. Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children. Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children. LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently. After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role. The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation. In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons. There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information. It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information. “We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.” A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. https://www.dw.com/en/police-raid-the-ma.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OIEz The police raided Halk TV in the middle of a live broadcast Image: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement On Wednesday morning, the live broadcast was halted , Halk TV's headquarters in the city of Istanbul were searched, and a new administrator was appointed by the government to run the media outlet. An arrest warrant was issued for the station's CEO, Cafer Mahiroglu, who currently lives in London. According to prosecutors, 11 people were arrested. Turkey has faced criticism for years over restrictions on press freedom . Halk TV is one of the country's best-known opposition television stations and regularly broadcasts critical reports about Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Justice and Development Party (AKP) . After the raid, journalists were initially prevented from entering the building. Pre-recorded programs were broadcast instead of live reports. The timing is particularly sensitive: Halk TV was raided on the very day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoglu was scheduled to begin his defense against corruption charges in court. The channel has been an important source of information for those following the trial. Imamoglu, who won the mayoral election in Istanbul in 2019 and remained in office until his arrest on March 19, 2025 , is one of Erdogan's most significant rivals, considered a beacon of hope for the opposition. He is still expected to run for president in 2028. He is accused of establishing and running a criminal organization, as well as of various related financial crimes. Prosecutors are seeking a prison term of 2,352 years related to 142 charges. Imamoglu denies the allegations, arguing that the case is politically motivated. 11 people were arrested in conjunction with the raid on Halk TV headquarters Image: ANKA Raid linked to investigation into Cafer Mahiroglu Istanbul prosecutors said that the raid on Halk TV was linked to an investigation into its CEO Mahiroglu, who is accused of bribery, bid rigging and money laundering. They said that arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people, on top of the 11 arrests. Assets belonging to companies allegedly linked to Mahiroglu were also seized and a trustee appointed to run the firms. The opposition responded with sharp criticism of the police raid. Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the social democratic New Party (Yeni Parti) said it was a dark day for Turkey. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," Mahiroglu said. "Showing solidarity with Halk TV means supporting the struggle for democracy in Turkey ," Ozel said. He added that "only dictators" would launch "a dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee […]" and criticized the fact that this had occurred on the day that Imamoglu was due to begin his defense. Many people in Turkey protested in support of Ekrem Imamoglu when he was jailed in 2025, like here in Izmir on May 19, 2025 Image: Berkcan Zengin/Middle East Images/picture alliance Journalists' union slams raid The Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS) also condemned the raid on the platform X, describing it as arbitrary and arguing that the press was free and should not be censored. Editor-in-chief Suat Toktas tried in vain to persuade the new state-appointed administrator to continue live broadcasts. In a video released by the TV channel, he said that what was happening was "illegal." Halk TV began broadcasting on January 10, 2005 and its live broadcasts gained widespread attention particularly during the 2013 Gezi Park protests. Cafer Mahiroglu took over the station in 2020. But little things matter too in the here and now, often disproportionately, and Andy Burnham, more than his predecessors, has decided that what he calls “everyday fixes” are worth focusing on too. Alexandra Topping wrote a good analysis about the pluses and minuses of this approach last week. But she filed too soon, because this morning Burnham has announced another five. These are all changes contained in tomorrow’s budget but being announced today – presumably because John Healey will have bigger surprises for MPs tomorrow, and the Treasury wants these measures to get some media attention today because tomorrow they will be overshadowed by another story. https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text: The Tunturi-Kiekko ice hockey team, based in Finland close to its most northerly border crossing with Russia, play against a team in Nikel, Russia, shortly before the Covid pandemic. Photograph: Juha Valtonen View image in fullscreen The Tunturi-Kiekko ice hockey team, based in Finland close to its most northerly border crossing with Russia, play against a team in Nikel, Russia, shortly before the Covid pandemic. Photograph: Juha Valtonen Ice hockey War has upended Russian-Nordic friendships forged on Arctic ice hockey rinks. Can they ever recover? Ban on Russian teams competing internationally has been lifted but days of friendly relations between Norwegian, Finnish and Russia players are a distant – if fond – memory Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Tue 10 Nov 2026 06.00 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 06.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For years, playing ice hockey against teams from Russia was a central part of Janne Tervahauta’s social life. Through his team, Tunturi-Kiekko, based in Ivalo, a rural Arctic town close to Finland’s most northerly border crossing with Russia, he would travel around the Arctic with his teammates. But the Barents Hockey League went on hold during the pandemic, and after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, all contact with Russia was stopped. “This hockey league was amateur, and a kind of old guys league. But it was very important for us,” said Tervahauta, 51. Since the war he has not had any contact with Russian teams. “Of course it is very sad,” he said. “It was a very important league of Arctic people. To meet each other – and of course it is a way to see and travel in the north.” Before February 2022, ice hockey diplomacy was a normal part of daily life for people in northern Finland, Norway and Russia. From the European side, it was a perfect way to help thaw cross-border relations after the cold war. And Russia’s global prowess at the sport made it an important lever for the country to exert soft power; it is no coincidence that it is Vladimir Putin’s favourite sport. In North America, Russian players have long been among the best in the National Hockey League (NHL): the Russian star of the Washington Capitals, Alexander Ovechkin, is the league’s all-time leading goalscorer, while also being the founder of a pro-Putin “social movement” called PutinTeam. View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin and the Russian star of the Washington Capitals, Alexander Ovechkin (third from left), in 2015. Photograph: Mikhail Klimentyev/RIA Novosti/Reuters Now, although individual Russians still play in the NHL and in other competitive leagues throughout Europe, the Nordic people who have fond memories of competing against Russian teams find it difficult to imagine a world in which that kind of close social connection will again be possible. RoKi, the official team of Santa Claus, based in Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland, and who play in Finland’s second highest league, regularly used to collaborate with Russian teams. They played pre-season friendlies against them, and hosted summer training camps for Kontinental Hockey League (KHL) teams from across the border. “There was considerable cooperation between Finnish and Russian ice hockey,” said Mika Toivola, the chief executive of RoKi Hockey. “Finnish players played in Russia, Russian players played in Finland, and clubs also met in pre-season friendlies.” But all of that came crashing to a halt in February 2022, just four days after Finland beat Russian players to men’s ice hockey gold in the Beijing Winter Olympics. Since Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, the national sides have not played each other, Finland joined Nato and the long border between the two nations completely closed. View image in fullscreen Janne Tervahauta said the Barents Hockey League, which involved teams from Finland, Norway and Russia, was important to Arctic people as a way to meet people and travel. Photograph: Janne Tervahauta Despite this, in a major coup for Putin, the court of arbitration for sport has ordered the International Ice Hockey Federation to permit Russia to return to international competition before the men’s world championship in Germany in May. This has left Finland – and much of the ice hockey world – reeling, and underlined the immense pressure that Russia can bring to bear in this arena. In response, the head of the Finnish ice hockey association said it would boycott games against Russia. Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Czech Republic, Austria, Latvia and Canada have followed suit . Toivola agrees with the boycott. “At RoKi, we unequivocally condemn Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said. “We believe that allowing Russian national teams to return to major international tournaments is wrong while Russia continues its war of aggression.” While he hopes that “peaceful sporting cooperation” will one day again become possible between Finland and Russia, ending the war in Ukraine is the “first prerequisite” to starting the long journey to rebuilding trust and cooperation. View image in fullscreen Finland and Russia play in an ice hockey match in Moscow in December 2021. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP “We must also remember the Ukrainian players, clubs and families whose daily lives are affected by the war,” he said. “This discussion is about more than who gets to compete for a world championship.” But on a local level, individual connections and friendships that were formed through hockey are still missed. William Sjøstrand, from the Kirkenes Puckers, a Norwegian team in the Barents Hockey League and the subject of the documentary Puckers, expressed sadness at not playing Russian teams, with whom he maintains contact. “We wait for the time when we can restart our game,” he said. With Kirkenes so far from other Norwegian towns, while several Russian towns are comparatively close, ending cooperation with Russian ice hockey teams was a great loss. Margrethe Alnes, an adviser and project coordinator at Barents Secretariat, which organised the Barents Hockey League, said the project “created something unique”. “Very good friendships and activities both for grownups and children. It went on for at least 10 years.” She added: “If you find a joint activity that both sides are interested in and have a passion for it is a good basis to create friendships and networks across borders, to find common ground.” The last four years, she said, had destroyed much of what was created during that time and work that was done to break down prejudice. “It’s really sad that it’s all ended.
